en: Oṃ, homage to the Netratantra!
To that which has perceptible reality as its object, which acts for the welfare of the world, and which is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
Salutations to you, Śiva, the soul of all, the source of the three worlds, who has conquered both anger and the god of love.
Truly, I do not know whether you are beyond the range of even the words of Bṛhaspati, let alone those of one such as I;
nevertheless, my devotion remains fixed upon the chanting of your virtues.
Whatever he commands me to do, that I shall perform.
Since this entire world is pervaded by you through your eightfold forms— consisting of ether, moon, fire, wind, self, earth, water, and mind—
who else could there be here whom one might wish to speak of?
Who else is there equal to him in the loss of shame?
Just as you alone now sustain the course of the world through your own functions such as fortitude and the rest,
so it would be, O Lord, if there were anyone else in the universe.
Being free from envy, the virtuous do not say anything at all [that is harmful].
O Lord, even the Grandfather (Brahmā), Purandara (Indra), and Viṣṇu— who have cast away all darkness through yoga and are the foremost even throughout the three worlds—
do not know [this] even today, despite their diligent efforts.
"That it is yours—oh, what a great magical illusion!"
In the activity of bringing about the arising, persistence, and destruction of existents,
various conceptual constructions arise within you;
yet, established in equanimity, with all purposeful activity withdrawn, you remain.
You are neither Indra, nor Viṣṇu, nor even the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Some have resorted to consciousness alone as the ultimate reality, [conceiving it] as being without substrate and devoid of name and form;
others [resort to it] as purified through the conceptualization of the three realms.
They spoke, upholding the tenets of their own scriptures.
Those very principles of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* which the followers of Sāṃkhya have declared to be the causes for the arising of the entire world—
they too are indeed manifestations of your own all-encompassing power.
What is there on earth that has not been encompassed by your powers?
Eternal yet of a perishable nature, manifold yet one,
fierce yet tranquil, devoid of qualities yet bound by qualities,
subject to saṃsāra, a master yet powerless and lacking independence.
In this way, poets praise your lordship repeatedly.
Because you transcend the domain of speech due to being beyond all description,
you are called "emptiness" by some who hold false propositions;
yet others [call] you precisely that, because of the connection between the signifier and the signified.
They conceptually construct a tranquil state by means of its specific attributes.
Those who follow the Vedas call you alone the primordial, undivided Puruṣa at the beginning and end of the three worlds;
yet it is you again whom they recognize within the interval between creation and dissolution.
They said that the "net of saṃsāra" is that which has undergone transformation through birth.
When you yourself remain, having restrained the self within the self by means of the self alone, with all your powers withdrawn,
then indeed the entire world remains dissolved within you.
O Lord, as long as your desire to create arises once again.
O Lord, there is nothing else superior to you in this world; neither an atom nor anything great exists apart from you.
You are the soul of all, and this entire universe is composed of you alone.
Indeed, the entire world has been contained within [the Self], just as a thread is held by a jewel.
O Lord, those mental states which partake in the distinctions of pleasure and pain,
and those various transformations of the modifications of primordial matter (pradhāna)—
of these you are the cause at birth and again at dissolution.
He is the cause of all waters, like the ocean.
O Teacher of the Gods, when you yourself created the eight—
the ether, self, fire, wind, water, earth, moon, and sun—
for the sake of another in this world, surely you were the primal cause.
At that very moment, the axe was applied to the root of the entire tree.
The sage Akṣapāda, having forcibly divided your form into sixteen parts, praises it through the construction of his system of valid cognition;
he does so by means of the arrangement of categories such as substance, which encompass all distinct entities.
Indeed, you have been praised even by Kaṇabhuj in the Vaiśeṣika system.
Even though the power of the Infinite Power is unimpeded, it binds the Knower of the Field with the nets of the snares of worldly existence; yet,
by cutting away all the qualities completely with the sword of knowledge, [it liberates him].
Another brings a person face-to-face with liberation.
Alas, they call that state the cessation of all activity of existence, the most peaceful condition known as liberation;
yet there is another state characterized by persistence, emergence, and dissolution.
The virtuous say that it is yours alone which is subject to saṃsāra.
O Blessed One, even those who are virtuous, yet whose light of understanding has been struck down by the intense cataract of ignorance regarding Your faults,
do not abandon worldly existence so long as they are not guided by You alone.
Until they have been awakened by the rays of one's own power.
Secret, dwelling in the cave of the heart, unborn, supremely pure, one, all-pervading, the primordial seed of all speech— when correctly employed, it becomes the cause of all that is desired.
Others say to you: "Is it not indeed the reality of sound?"
Whatever these people, addicted to the practices of heretics, declare to be the truth after speculating with their own fancies—
that very thing is yours; there is nothing else at all.
Regarding these designations, there is merely this dispute among the learned.

O Lord, even the primordial teachers rightly [perceive] you alone as the seed of omniscience, unchanging and of undiminished power, the cause for establishing the path to both supreme beatitude and worldly prosperity.
Having propitiated them, they attained the greatness of the state of a Tīrthaṅkara.
Although omniscience is primarily attributed to another [the Buddha] by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
nevertheless, because you are the Supreme Lord,
even your sovereignty attains a non-figurative application.
Indeed, O Lord, it is because the state of being the creator of the world rests in you alone.
One person proceeds by means of the visible world of objects,
another by means of conventions of inference, and yet another by means of words; but for you, on the other hand, the object of perception exists all at once.
The entire range of objects of knowledge is known as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand.
O Lord, for this self which is a subject, whose activity is dependent on others, and who is distinct from the world and from primordial nature (prakṛti),
you alone are the supreme cause for its conjunction with and its cessation from [the world].
The driving force of the mechanism that turns the wheel of saṃsāra.
Even though he himself repeatedly performs actions prescribed by the scope of the scriptures with an unwearied intellect,
he is nevertheless joined with the fruit appropriate to them.
The incomparable fruit of that deed belongs to you alone.

By bestowing undesired results upon those who lack the power of enthusiasm, the crippled, the meritless, the dull-witted, those who have abandoned their commitments, the merciless, and the untruthful;
By you, the doctrine of the excellence of human effort has been discarded.
Actions prescribed by the Vedas bestow happiness after death, yet that fruit is finite;
in your teaching, however, there is infinite happiness free from all defects.
For they say that prostration performed with devotion leads to burning away [of karmic taints].
O Blessed One, when you manifest within yourself the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*), assuming forms anew at every moment,
even that [power] attains its true significance only in you.
For the most part, the doctrine of momentary flux was composed by those who were unrefined.

Having refuted those who claim that the state which cannot be attained by non-Buddhists through immeasurable births in this world is reached in their own systems through a single birth by means of intelligence, [the author says:]...
Indeed, you have placed your foot upon their heads.
Greedily covetous, with minds defiled and fallen from their commitments,
even those who are self-controlled become wicked when their minds are eclipsed by Rāhu through the mere assumption of the outward signs prescribed in your teaching.
"They are liberated"—this is your exceedingly great lion's roar.
O Blessed One, this unimpeded teaching of yours possesses a great and peerless power, like a wish-fulfilling gem;
for by receiving initiation performed according to the correct ritual procedure, [one attains the goal].
Indeed, even without knowledge, one attains isolation (kaivalya).
This knowledge, which is the seed of the fruit of liberation within the self, has been obscured by the latent tendencies of the bound soul;
yet, O Blessed One, it has been revealed by your scripture, as if by a rescuer.
It becomes accomplished for the sake of fulfilling the fruit of liberation.
When, after countless births, the disposition of a living being becomes exhausted [of defilements] through your desire for grace,
they cross beyond the net of saṃsāra and attain peace in you alone.
One reaches the ultimate state even if devoid of awakening.
This entire fourteenfold world,
the circle of saṃsāra divided by its internal distinctions—
you protect it, destroy it, and create it according to your will.
Thinking thus, the virtuous declare that one is not defiled.
Unimpeded sovereignty, innate dispassion, contentment born of one's very nature, mastery over the senses,
ultimate bliss, and unobstructed power.
And knowledge regarding all objects belongs to you alone, O Blessed One.

For even those who have diligently acquired the darkness [of ignorance], you have led them—alas!—to that ultimate happiness which is so difficult to attain, wherein all suffering is cast away; even those who were like donkeys, camels, and trees! Oh, what a marvel!
His sovereignty is unimpeded even throughout the three worlds.
This is the incomparable fruit of that drop of semen of yours, by which the entire Mount Sumeru was turned to gold as it fell, its canopy of crest-jewels shimmering with stainless light.
The world obtained that which was the golden ornament of one [person].
Having correctly understood that the meritless karma accumulated over time— which for three kalpas had become the very structure of the triple world— has been burnt away by you, who would not [bow]?
Except for a fool, there is no partiality toward you.
The Kālakūṭa poison, born from the churning of the essence of the Ocean of Milk and terrifying the assembly of the gods—
drink it without envy for the welfare of the world.
Indeed, every word of praise has been received by you alone.
O Blessed One, although you are peaceful in nature, you have forcibly consumed desire with the fire born from your eyes;
for even among the great, a transgression, however small, is not to be overlooked.
I believe that the ripening [of karma] has been described as harsh for people.
O Blessed One, although you placed your beloved in half of your own body out of affection,
you alone remain the foremost among mortals for your deeds that cause wonder throughout the three worlds.
Even today, no one at all imitates him.
By him, through the power generated by the majesty of yoga, this entire world was cast down from its lofty height;
that son of Prajāpati has been forcibly seized.
"Alas! Who would not be filled with wonder here at such pride on your part?"
He whose life-breaths did not suddenly depart even when crushed by your thumb—
how is it that he alone was conquered by Hari only after a long time and with great effort?
Since he is Daśānana by nature, where indeed is this cause for wonder?
The Mandākinī, its waters perfumed by golden lotuses and pārijāta flowers, falling from the sky,
clings to the tips of his matted locks like a drop of frost.
By whom else, other than you, has he been supported and favored?
Let alone your other incomparable sovereignty which serves as the cause for the title of "Lord";
O Blessed One, even your lineage has not reached its end.
If even Viṣṇu, together with the Grandfather [Brahmā], is unable to do so, how much less could anyone else?
Of Śveta, who, though standing at the moment of his execution like an animal at the slaughterhouse, was within the reach of Mṛtyudamana himself—
you have provided protection by seizing him and restraining him.
To whom in this world does that not cause sufficient wonder?
O Lord, just as Upamanyu was freed from his resentment and favored by you through the distribution of the milk-ocean,
so it would be if there were anyone else in this world who was your equal.
Having cast off stinginess, these virtuous ones proclaim thus.
In that same manner, you, laughing, paralyzed the power of the arm of the enemy of Vṛtra as it brandished its thunderbolt;
likewise, you did the same to the teeth of Pūṣan and to the eyes of Bhaga.
And Dakṣa’s sense of ownership regarding the fruit of his sacrifice was cast away.

Just as in this world, O Paśupati, the worlds of Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Purandara, along with the guardians of the quarters, animals, gods, asuras, humans, and other divine beings, have been fashioned by you.
In the same way, tell me, whose other stations are they?
Even while Kṛṣṇa— the son of Śakra, who holds the Śārṅga bow and the discus in his hands and has already shattered the lord of the Dānavas— stood present,
[Arjuna] was tormented by the fear of Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Karṇa.
O Śaṅkara, you have brought about a state of extreme tranquility for Arjuna.
O Blessed One, by you who were propitiated and who showered a rain of gold for King Marutta as he desired to sacrifice—
those acts of grace toward your devotees which were proclaimed throughout the world;
Therefore, O Lord, that supreme lordship of yours has not been praised.

When you were pleased and granted protection to that descendant of Bhṛgu, Śukra, whose every sense was tormented by the falling of grain-dust and smoke due to his intense vows; at that time, he was Śukra.
Shining in the sky amidst clouds of cold, heat, and wind.
While you protect these worlds by dividing yourself,
let this incomparable majesty of yours remain;
even your offspring of Dakṣa within these three worlds [is subject to your power].
No one knows what dispute you have with him.

O Protector of the World, compassionate toward those who seek refuge from fear, you are one who wanders on the wrong path, slow in discerning virtues and faults, fierce, defiled, unrestrained, and of little essence.
O Lord, be gracious; please purify this mind of mine.
O Lord, these senses are fickle, evil-intentioned, greedy,
and bound to delightful objects;
like unrestrained horses, they are difficult to control because of their rebellious nature.
Always bring my six sense faculties under my control.
When Nandīśvara, though being a human being, was brought by time to death in the utmost extremity before long,
he acted with equanimity toward all things out of contentment.
This was not a marvel in the past, nor will it be so in the future; it does not exist [as a marvel] at present.
O Lord, this mind of mine is subject to the snare of saṃsāra, powerless, deluded, its light obscured by the darkness of false reasoning— O Destroyer of Manmatha, O Burner of Time!
O God of gods, lead me upon the path frequented by the virtuous.
Being deluded, I am being destroyed individually by various misfortunes that cling to the body, and by passion and other afflictions that have taken hold within the mind.
Tell me, who other than you shall I go for refuge?
Indeed, for one who is seized by the demon of desire that causes exhaustion, and further by the unbridled seizure of anger,
and whose intellect is thus distressed, this is for the sake of liberation.
Whatever task is mine to perform here, that is within your power alone.
O Lord, that very craving which has been the cause of the world’s contempt and the reason for even the Lord of the Gods’ own humiliation,
always mocks me.
Break it by force, O Blessed One, so that there is no further becoming.
O Blessed One, sever by force that which veils this beast so that its power of consciousness is stolen,
whereby it does not know the reality that is beneficial to itself or to the world—
sever all of that for me.
Let the darkness born of ignorance be dispelled by the Great Light.

As long as this body of mine does not perish— this abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking self-mastery, prone to sudden downfall, devoid of discernment, and perceived as essence-less— [I shall strive for liberation].
O Lord, employ them accordingly in virtuous deeds.
Since even the Lotus-born Brahmā grows weary while praising you directly with all four of his mouths,
what are we compared to in the task of extolling your virtues?
Devotion is the authority; forgive all of this.

O sole friend of the world, O you named Avadhūta, whatever slight merit has been acquired here by me through this hymn of praise offered with devotion according to my own intellectual capacity— [May it lead to the attainment of the state of the Awakened.]
Therefore, O Blessed One, let the world have devotion toward you.
Thus ends the hymn to the Lord’s devotion composed by the illustrious Avadhūtasiddha.
